problematic_sentences.text: From 2018 to 2021, DWS made materially misleading statements about its controls for incorporating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into research and investment recommendations for ESG‑integrated products.

DWS marketed itself as a ‘leader in ESG’ and stated that ESG was in its ‘DNA’, yet the firm failed to adequately implement its ESG integration policy and failed to adopt and implement policies and procedures to ensure that its public statements about its ESG integration were accurate.

The first poster featured an aerial image of waves crashing on a shore with text that stated ‘Climate change doesn’t do borders. Neither do rising sea levels. That’s why HSBC is aiming to provide up to $1 trillion in financing and investment globally to help our clients transition to net zero’.

The second poster featured an image of tree growth rings with text that stated ‘Climate changes doesn’t do borders. So in the UK, we’re helping to plant 2 million trees which will lock in 1.25 million tonnes of carbon over their lifetime’.

We considered consumers would understand the claims “HSBC is aiming to provide up to $1 trillion in financing and investment globally to help our clients transition to net zero” in ad (a) and “we’re helping to plant 2 million trees which will lock in 1.25 million tonnes of carbon in their lifetime” in ad (b) to mean that HSBC was making, and intended to make, a positive overall environmental contribution as a company.

We did not consider that consumers would understand the intricacies of transitioning to net zero, and would not expect that HSBC, in making unqualified claims about its environmentally beneficial work, would also be simultaneously involved in the financing of businesses which made significant contributions to carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gas emissions and would continue to do so for many years into the future.
The CAP Code required that the basis of environmental claims must be clear and that unqualified claims could mislead if they omit significant information.

HSBC UK Bank plc said it had been making the claim in ad (a) since 2020 and aimed to meet the ambition to provide financing and investment globally to help some of its clients transition to net zero by 2030.

HSBC said that the financing of greenhouse gas‑emitting industries was required during the transition to net zero, and so their continued financing of those industries was not in conflict with the aims of a transition to net zero.

HSBC said that the ads did not mislead about HSBC’s total environmental impact and invited consumers to find out more about the initiatives through a call to action – “Search HSBC Sustainability”; they said that consumers who searched for those terms would find a detailed summary of climate change initiatives and the Climate Strategy on their website.

The Annual Report indicated that HSBC intended to invest between $750 billion and $1 trillion in helping its clients transition to net zero, but also indicated that its current financed emissions stood at around 65.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year for oil and gas alone and that figure was likely to be much higher once other carbon‑intensive industries were included; we also understood from the Annual Report that HSBC intended to continue funding thermal coal mining and power production to some degree until 2040 (or 2030 in the OECD).

The complaint concerned statements made in several advertisements by Shell, including a television commercial, in which the company said: “Change, we have to, we can, we want to, and so Shell is investing in new energy for the Netherlands; we are developing hydrogen for the regional buses and trucks of tomorrow; we are changing for a cleaner future”.

We are changing for a cleaner future; to keep the Netherlands warm, operational and moving, Shell is active in oil and gas, but we are changing for a cleaner future; we have to, we can and we want to; therefore, Shell also invests in new energy for the Netherlands, for example through electric transport, hydrogen and biofuels.
We are building wind turbine parks at sea, with smart extras to generate electricity even when the wind isn’t strong; this allows us to make green energy from wind at sea for homes and businesses.

The original complaint against Shell’s statements was that they were in breach of Article 3.1 and 3.2 of the Dutch Sustainability Claims Code, which requires sustainability claims to be clear, specific, correct and unambiguous and prohibits advertising an aspiration when it cannot reasonably be suspected that this will be attained.

Shell breached these requirements with its statements, as Shell’s plans to reduce the production of fossil fuels have been reversed, its investments in renewable energy are only a small fraction of its total budget, and its advertised ‘sustainable’ actions contribute little to nothing to reducing Shell’s emissions.

However, the Advertising Code Committee decided that Shell’s advertisements made sufficiently clear that Shell’s efforts were mere aspirations, as required under Article 3.2 SCC, and argued that it was clear on the face of the advertisements that Shell is in a transition process and that their plans haven’t yet come to fruition.

The Committee states that Shell is entitled to advertise its concrete projects with biofuels, hydrogen, electric charging points and the capture of CO2 and that the complainant didn’t provide any evidence that Shell is not investing in these projects; overall, the Committee held that there was no violation, emphasising that the average consumer would understand the nuanced approach taken by Shell.

The appellant maintains that Shell’s current advertisements need to be viewed in light of its decades‑long efforts to advertise its ‘sustainable’ activities, which may have allowed consumers to think that Shell is making a significant effort to green its operations; in reality, Shell’s sustainability projects are but a fraction of the entirety of its operations, and as such the appellant argued that Shell should place its sustainability advertisements within their rightful context.

By failing to apply Article 3.1 SCC, the Committee didn’t test whether Shell’s advertisements were sufficiently substantiated, nuanced and specified; Shell provides no context as to what it means to be ‘changing’ or to become ‘cleaner’.

The Committee assumes that the advertisements convey Shell’s ambitions within each advertised project; however, as Shell provides multiple projects for its ambition to ‘change for a cleaner future’, such as investing in biofuels and carbon capture, the interpretation of the ‘concreteness’ of Shell’s plan should encompass its entire ambition to ‘change for a cleaner future’, not just within the context of a single project.

Shell’s emission reduction targets to lower Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 50% in 2030 are not clear from the advertisements; the advertisements merely convey that Shell invests in sustainable projects, but they do not clarify what Shell’s aspirations are other than a ‘cleaner future’, making it difficult for consumers to understand whether a project is part of Shell’s 2030 or 2050 emissions reduction target or pursued for another reason, and therefore the Board of Appeal deems Shell’s advertisements to be in violation of Article 3.2 SCC.
You cannot advertise an aspiration when it cannot reasonably be suspected that this will be attained.
It is argued that the Committee overestimates the knowledgeability of the regular consumer regarding Shell’s activities.
The Board of Appeal disagreed with the appellant that Shell’s advertisements would confuse a regular consumer as to what Shell’s operations entail.

HSBC believed the claims in ads (a) and (b) highlighted two tangible and specific short‑to‑medium term initiatives, capable of quantifiable measurement, and would not be seen as commenting, in a broader sense, on their green credentials or environmental contribution.

Consumers could access HSBC’s climate change initiatives and Climate Strategy via the “Search HSBC Sustainability” call to action on the ads; the bank argued that this meant the ads did not mislead about its total environmental impact.
We have learned from the ongoing changing regulatory environment and our own findings and continue to improve our ESG governance, processes and controls.

unproblematic_sentences.text: Electricity from renewable sources: source 100% renewable electricity by 2025, with an interim ambition of 85% by 2022.
Achieve 32% of positions at the first management level below the Executive Board held by female executives and 33% at the second management level below the Executive Board by 2024.
DS Smith has a science‑based target requiring at least a 40% reduction in carbon emissions per tonne of production by 2030 compared to 2019 and has committed to net‑zero emissions by 2050.

The Met Office clearly set out how emissions metrics and targets have been set and measured throughout the period, including their initial stocktake to calculate their baseline, the GHG Protocol methodology used, and the metrics and targets selected to drive key change.

Where organisations have set their own net zero or carbon neutral targets, an explanation of what this means – including baselines, how they plan to achieve it and progress so far – is important to allow users to assess performance.

Forward‑looking good practice requires that future targets, goals and commitments include appropriate interim targets with performance tracked, supported by charts with trajectory lines and accompanied by narrative comparing performance to prior periods and actions undertaken.

Good practice reports fairly assess the likelihood of meeting goals or commitments, clearly identify where performance is behind target and include trajectory lines continuing until the end commitment date, avoiding overly positive commentary.

The guide notes that organisations should consider emissions from other specific KPIs, such as supplier engagement scores, with an accompanying fair and balanced assessment of supplier performance including both successes and ongoing challenges.
UKRI includes forward‑looking trend lines to the end of the GGC commitment period so users can easily assess performance against the target and the likelihood of meeting the commitment.

UKRI’s GGC charts and graphs clearly demonstrate performance against target during the current and past periods, with trajectory lines continuing until the end commitment or goal completion date and narrative clearly identifying where performance was behind target and explaining why.

Accurate and transparent reporting of climate and environmental metrics and targets is essential for accountability and demonstrating central government’s commitment to sustainability; by setting clear, measurable targets and consistently reporting on key metrics, government bodies enhance transparency and drive performance improvements.

Organisations should include historic, baseline and target information when visually representing data and should ensure consistent frameworks and data collection methods each year to facilitate comparability.
unproblematic_sentences.source_section: Metrics and targets – charts and tables

unproblematic_sentences.text: Good practice sustainability reporting provides a fair and honest explanation when performance is off track, with narrative comparing performance to prior periods and linking to actions undertaken.

The guide emphasises that good practice includes the inclusion of a target trajectory line continuing until the end commitment or goal completion date, accompanied by a narrative that fairly assesses the likelihood of meeting the goal based on current performance and trajectories.
The guide states that organisations should clearly set out how emissions metrics and targets are set and measured, including baseline calculations and methodology used such as the GHG Protocol.

The Met Office explains their carbon neutral commitments appropriately in the annual report, including organisation‑specific metrics and targets beyond headline net‑zero statements and emissions targets, and links climate‑related metrics and targets to the risks and opportunities to which they relate.

The Department for Transport integrates climate adaptation into broader organisational objectives, provides transparency about future climate risks and signposts to supplementary information, helping readers understand the organisation’s long‑term resilience.

UK Research and Innovation identifies climate change as a principal risk and provides supporting risk information, demonstrating good practice in linking risk identification to sustainability reporting.

Government bodies should consider Scope 3 emissions and provide clear methodology, set SMART targets and provide historical data to avoid unsubstantiated net‑zero commitments or cherry‑picking positive data.

In 2024, we achieved a 20% reduction from 2023 levels, resulting in a cumulative 56% reduction from the 2019 baseline, achieving the 50% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions target ahead of schedule; we aim to further reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 65% from 2019 levels by 2030.

To fulfil our GHG reduction objectives, we have and continue to actively reduce our operational carbon footprint through the reduced consumption of greenhouse gas emitting resources; this includes enhancing operational efficiencies, identifying renewable energy opportunities across our real estate portfolio and leveraging key learnings from 2020 to increase emission reduction rates during the return‑to‑office transition.

We have adapted and reimagined our offices to support the evolving workplace dynamics to support our employees globally as they connect and collaborate in hybrid, in‑office or work‑from‑home environments, and this adaptability plays a crucial role in our overall reduction of GHG emissions.

At Liberty, these debates have had little impact on our climate actions as our climate strategy is closely aligned with our core purpose of supporting clients with risk identification, risk mitigation and risk transfer; throughout the year we have continued to prioritise projects that support the integration of climate consideration into our business strategy and decision‑making.

These projects include refining our approach to climate resiliency by focusing on the built environment and resilient infrastructure, continuing research and investment in enhancing our modelling capabilities through a bespoke portfolio‑level transition risk model that leverages NGFS data and advancing new insights on high‑priority perils such as hurricane frequency, flood and wildfire risk, sharing our expertise through a Physical Climate Risk Management Framework and hosting the Geneva Association’s Climate Change and Environment Conference, and expanding our Climate Activation Programme globally with leadership participation and tailored sessions for product leaders.

In 2025, we see the world moving in a disorderly transition with each region and country pursuing its own policy and strategy; as the world experiences increased physical climate risk we anticipate and welcome shifts toward a greater need for climate resiliency and will continue to execute our strategy and support our customers globally wherever they are in their transition journey.

At Liberty Mutual, the Board of Directors oversees the ongoing development of our enterprise‑level business strategy and the management and implementation of our climate strategy, with responsibilities delegated to the Risk Committee and Governance and Sustainability Committee.

We continue to enhance our governance structure to support communication, collaboration and effective decision‑making, ensuring that climate‑related financial risks and opportunities are understood by our Board of Directors and across every level of our business.

GE Aerospace has an ambition to achieve net‑zero Scope 3 emissions from the use of sold products by 2050 and notes that its current engines are around 40% more fuel efficient than engines designed in the 1970s and 1980s, with the RISE programme aiming to develop technologies that enable engines to be at least 20% more fuel efficient and emit 20% fewer CO2 emissions than today’s most efficient engines.

Merck’s board of directors oversees ESG matters and has established a cross‑functional EHS Council composed of senior leaders to manage climate‑related issues; the company applies scenario analysis using the Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5 scenario to assess physical risks for ten key facilities across various hazards.

Merck’s risk management process includes identifying, assessing and managing climate‑related risks across at least ten facilities using advanced modelling to evaluate hazards like high temperature, wildfires, drought, storm surge and sea level rise, with results informing adaptation measures and investment decisions.

Banner Bank has established board‑level oversight of climate‑related risks with a risk committee that reviews policies and risk assessments, and its directors receive ESG training to ensure adequate understanding of climate risk and opportunities.

AT&T aims to reduce absolute Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 63% by 2030 from a 2015 baseline and achieve net‑zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2035; by 2022 its emissions were approximately 4.8 million metric tonnes of CO2e, a reduction of over 4 million metric tonnes from 2015 (over 45%).
AT&T aims for 50% of suppliers to set science‑based targets by 2024 and reported that 53% of suppliers had done so by 2022.

AT&T’s Gigaton Goal aims to enable its customers to save 1 billion metric tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions by 2035, and by 2022 the company reported that customers had avoided 149.2 million metric tonnes through its products and services.

Liberty Mutual continues research and investment in enhancing its modelling capabilities, building a bespoke portfolio‑level transition risk model that leverages NGFS data and advancing insights on high‑priority perils including hurricane frequency, flood and wildfire risk.

Liberty Mutual shares its expertise on managing physical climate risk through the publication of a Physical Climate Risk Management Framework and by hosting the Geneva Association’s Climate Change and Environment Conference to facilitate industry‑wide dialogue on climate.

Liberty Mutual has expanded its Climate Activation Programme globally with new leadership participation, tailored sessions to engage product leaders and the development of new content and online training modules.

We continue to prioritise projects that support the integration of climate considerations into our business strategy and decision‑making, including refining our approach to climate resiliency and enhancing modelling capabilities.
